title: Discovery Walk — Core Method
description: An inventory scan begins with a discovery walk: traverse the archive's namespace depth-first, listing every collection, file, and database encountered. The walk is iterative rather than recursive so it cannot overflow on pathological nesting, and it records the path of everything it sees. Symbolic links and aliases are noted but not followed twice, which keeps cyclic namespaces from looping forever. The walk's output — the raw census of what exists — feeds every later inventory stage. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
NS = {"arc": ["db1", "db2"], "db1": ["c1", "c2"], "db2": ["c3"]}
stack, seen, order = ["arc"], set(), []
while stack:
    node = stack.pop()
    if node in seen: continue
    seen.add(node); order.append(node)
    stack.extend(NS.get(node, []))
print("discovered:", sorted(order))

title: Type-Size-Count Census — Core Method
description: For each discovered resource the scanner records its type, byte size, and record count, aggregating into a census: so many databases, so many files, so many bytes per format. Sizes come from metadata where trustworthy and from sampling where they are not, with the method noted per resource. The census answers capacity questions — how big is the archive, where is the weight — that no per-record view can. Repeating the census over time also reveals growth rates, which drive storage planning. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Access-Condition Probing — Core Method
description: Knowing a resource exists is not knowing you can read it: the scanner probes access conditions — open, credentialed, embargoed, or restricted — with a harmless metadata read rather than a full fetch. Each resource is labeled with its condition and the credential class required, so search planners skip what they cannot open. Probes are rate-limited and cached, because hammering ten thousand databases with access checks is itself a denial of service. The access map this produces is as important as the inventory itself. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Incremental Rescan — Core Method
description: Full rescans of a boundless archive are prohibitively expensive, so the scanner checkpoints its progress and later rescans only what changed: new resources, resized files, altered access conditions. Change detection uses modification stamps and content hashes recorded during the previous scan. The delta is merged into the stored inventory, keeping it fresh at a fraction of the cost. Incremental scanning is what makes continuous inventory practical instead of a monthly batch ordeal. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Inventory Reporting — Core Method
description: The scan is only useful if its results can be read: the reporter renders the census, access map, and deltas into a structured report with totals, top formats by bytes, and flagged anomalies like sudden size drops. Reports are versioned and diffable, so 'what changed since last month' is one command. Machine-readable and human-readable forms are generated from the same data to avoid drift between them. A good inventory report is the archive's annual physical — boring when healthy, invaluable when not. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
